# Quantum Propagation of Massive Scalar Fields in an Expanding Universe

This study investigates the quantum propagation of a doublet of massive scalar fields within the context of an expanding universe, one that may be filled with radiation. The central focus of this investigation lies in understanding the dissipative effects that arise in connection with the rate of cosmic expansion. By examining how these fields evolve and decay in a dynamical spacetime background, the work aims to illuminate the interplay between quantum field behavior and the large-scale geometry of the cosmos.

At first order in the analysis, the results confirm an expected and well-established outcome: the decay rate of the scalar fields is determined by the local temperature of the surrounding environment. This finding aligns with standard predictions from thermal field theory, in which the ambient temperature governs the dissipative dynamics of propagating particles.

Moving beyond the linear approximation, however, the analysis reveals a more nuanced picture. At higher orders, the decay rate acquires an additional contribution that is governed by the expansion parameter of the universe. This term reflects the influence of the cosmic expansion itself on the quantum dynamics of the fields, introducing a dissipative effect that is distinct from the purely thermal contribution identified at first order.

Notably, this expansion-related contribution does not vanish in the absence of a thermal background. Even for stable particles propagating in the vacuum, the effect persists, indicating that the expansion of the universe imparts a fundamental dissipative character to quantum propagation that is independent of any surrounding radiation. This result underscores the profound impact that a dynamical spacetime can have on quantum fields, even under otherwise idealized conditions.

Finally, the authors examine the long-time behavior of the propagator, tracing how the quantum correlations of the fields evolve over extended timescales. Building on this analysis, they discuss the implications of their findings for the trans-Planckian question—the problem of how physics at extremely short distances, potentially beyond the Planck scale, may influence observable phenomena. Through this discussion, the study connects its formal results to one of the outstanding conceptual challenges in modern cosmology and high-energy physics.

# Quantum Particle Propagation in Expanding Cosmological Backgrounds

## Introduction and Motivation

The behavior of quantum fields in curved, time-dependent spacetimes remains one of the central problems at the interface of quantum field theory and cosmology. When particles propagate through an expanding universe, the underlying geometry is no longer static, and the familiar notions of particle states, vacuum, and stability must be re-examined. In this work, we investigate the propagation of quantum particles in expanding cosmological backgrounds by analyzing a doublet of massive scalar fields, with particular attention to scenarios in which the universe is filled with radiation. Our primary focus lies in the dissipative effects that emerge as a direct consequence of the cosmic expansion rate.

## Setup and Framework

We consider a system consisting of two coupled massive scalar fields—a doublet—evolving in a Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) geometry. The choice of a doublet structure allows us to capture nontrivial mixing and interaction effects that would be absent in a single-field treatment, while the massive character of the fields ensures that the particles possess a well-defined rest frame and dispersion relation in the appropriate limit. By allowing the background to be radiation-filled, we connect our analysis to physically relevant epochs of cosmological history, where the expansion is driven by relativistic matter.

The expansion of the universe introduces a time-dependent scale factor, whose rate of change—the Hubble parameter—governs the coupling between the quantum fields and the geometric background. It is precisely this expansion rate that serves as the control parameter for the dissipative phenomena we uncover.

## Dissipative Effects Beyond Linear Order

At linear order in perturbation theory, the propagation of particles in such a background reproduces the expected behavior, with damping and redshifting effects that are well understood. However, when we extend the analysis beyond linear order, a qualitatively new feature emerges. We find that the decay rate of the particles acquires an additional contribution that is directly governed by the expansion parameter.

Remarkably, this contribution persists even for particles that would be perfectly stable in flat, vacuum spacetime. In other words, the expansion of the universe itself induces an effective dissipation, causing states that are otherwise protected against decay to exhibit a nonzero decay rate. This is a genuinely gravitational, or cosmological, effect: it originates not from any intrinsic instability of the field content but from the interplay between the quantum dynamics and the time-dependent geometry.

## Implications for the Long-Time Propagator

The appearance of this expansion-induced decay rate has direct and significant consequences for the structure of the propagator at late times. The long-time behavior of the two-point function is modified relative to the standard expectation, reflecting the accumulated effect of the dissipation over the course of cosmic evolution. This modification alters the way correlations decay and persist, and it must be taken into account in any careful treatment of quantum coherence in an expanding universe.

## Connection to the Trans-Planckian Question

Finally, our findings bear directly on the trans-Planckian question—the concern that modes observed today may have originated at wavelengths far below the Planck scale in the early universe, where the applicability of standard field-theoretic assumptions is uncertain. The expansion-driven dissipative contribution we identify offers a new perspective on how physics at these extreme scales might imprint itself on observable quantities. By tying the modification of the decay rate to the expansion parameter, our analysis provides a concrete mechanism through which trans-Planckian effects could manifest in the long-time propagator, thereby offering a potential handle on this longstanding conceptual issue.

## Conclusion

In summary, by studying a doublet of massive scalar fields in an expanding, possibly radiation-filled, cosmological background, we have identified a dissipative effect tied to the expansion rate that appears beyond linear order. This effect endows even stable particles with a nonvanishing decay rate, reshapes the long-time behavior of the propagator, and carries meaningful implications for the trans-Planckian question. These results underscore the subtle and physically rich consequences of quantum propagation in dynamical spacetimes.

# Abstract

We investigate the quantum dynamics of a massive scalar field propagating in a spatially flat Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker spacetime, with particular emphasis on the dissipative effects induced by the cosmological expansion. By recasting the mode equations in terms of a time-dependent effective frequency, we demonstrate that the Hubble expansion rate acts as an effective friction term that damps field oscillations and drives the system out of adiabatic equilibrium. We derive exact and approximate solutions for the mode functions across the transition from sub-horizon to super-horizon scales, showing how the competition between the field mass, the comoving wavenumber, and the expansion rate governs the amplitude and phase evolution of quantum fluctuations. Working within the framework of the in-in formalism, we compute the two-point correlation functions and quantify the departure from the adiabatic vacuum through the Bogoliubov coefficients, which encode the rate of gravitational particle production. Our analysis reveals that the expansion-induced dissipation manifests as an effective decoherence of the field modes, with the associated entropy production scaling nontrivially with the ratio of the field mass to the Hubble scale. We further examine the backreaction of the produced quanta on the background dynamics and discuss the regime of validity of the semiclassical approximation. These results clarify the interplay between quantum coherence and cosmological dissipation, with implications for the generation of primordial perturbations, the thermalization of early-universe fields, and the emergence of classical behavior from quantum initial conditions.

# Abstract

We investigate the decay rates of scalar particles propagating in cosmological backgrounds, focusing on the interplay between thermal effects and spacetime expansion. Working within a curved-spacetime quantum field theory framework, we compute the modified decay width of a massive scalar field in a Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) geometry, incorporating finite-temperature corrections through the thermal field theory formalism. Our analysis reveals that the expansion of the universe introduces a time-dependent shift in the decay rate relative to the flat-space result, while temperature contributions enhance the rate through Bose-Einstein statistical factors and induced processes forbidden in vacuum. We derive explicit expressions for the decay rate as a function of the Hubble parameter and background temperature, identifying regimes in which curvature and thermal effects dominate. In the ultraviolet limit, we examine trans-Planckian implications, showing how physics beyond the Planck scale may modify the dispersion relations and, consequently, the predicted decay rates. We discuss the sensitivity of observable quantities to such trans-Planckian modifications and comment on potential imprints in the early-universe particle spectrum and cosmological observables. These results provide a consistent framework for evaluating particle decays during inflationary and radiation-dominated epochs, with relevance for reheating dynamics and dark-matter production scenarios.

---

*Keywords:* scalar field decay, curved spacetime, finite-temperature field theory, cosmological expansion, trans-Planckian physics

I'd be happy to help you structure these results, though I should note upfront that the specific quantitative results (exact decay rates, precise scaling exponents) will depend on your particular model setup—the scalar potential, the coupling structure of your doublet, and your conventions. Let me offer a framework and flag where you'll need to insert your own derivations.

## Decay Rates

For a doublet of massive scalars in a radiation-dominated FRW background, key considerations to address abstractly:

- **Hubble dilution vs. intrinsic decay**: The effective decay of field amplitudes typically combines the intrinsic mass-driven oscillation/decay with the Hubble friction term (∝ 3H φ̇). In radiation domination, H ∝ 1/(2t), which modifies naive Minkowski decay rates.
- **Doublet structure**: You'll want to specify whether the two fields have a mass splitting, mixing, or a symmetry (e.g., an internal SU(2) or U(1)) that protects certain channels. This determines whether decay proceeds through inter-doublet transitions.

## Propagator Long-Time Behavior

- In an expanding background the propagator generally loses time-translation invariance, so you'll be working with a two-time object G(t, t').
- The long-time asymptotics often show power-law modulation of the flat-space oscillatory/exponential behavior, inherited from the scale factor a(t) ∝ t^(1/2) in radiation domination.

## The Trans-Planckian Question

This concerns whether modes that are sub-Planckian today originated at trans-Planckian physical wavelengths at early times, and whether your results depend sensitively on unknown UV physics.

---

1. Your action/Lagrangian and the doublet's internal symmetry

# Quantum Field Propagation and Dissipation in Expanding Spacetime

**Abstract**

We investigate the propagation and dissipative dynamics of quantum fields in a spatially flat Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker background, focusing on corrections to particle decay rates induced by cosmological expansion. Employing the closed-time-path formalism, we derive the effective equation of motion for a scalar field coupled to a thermal environment, extracting the self-energy contributions that govern dissipation. At first order in the coupling, we recover a Hubble-modified decay rate exhibiting characteristic redshift suppression relative to the Minkowski result. Beyond linear order, we identify non-trivial memory effects and higher-order vertex corrections that break the naive adiabatic approximation, yielding time-dependent widths sensitive to the expansion history. Our analysis reveals that beyond-linear-order corrections can either enhance or suppress dissipation depending on the ratio of the Hubble parameter to the field mass. These results have implications for reheating, dark matter freeze-in, and the thermalization of primordial fields, providing a systematic framework for non-equilibrium quantum field theory in curved spacetime.

We investigate the dynamics of a scalar field doublet propagating in an expanding cosmological background, with particular attention to its decay properties and long-time behavior. Working within a systematic expansion scheme, we demonstrate that the decay rate of the field is governed by the local temperature at first order, consistent with expectations from thermal field theory in curved spacetime. Extending our analysis beyond linear order, we identify an additional expansion-dependent contribution to the effective decay rate that persists even for particles that would remain stable in the vacuum, indicating that cosmological expansion itself induces non-trivial dissipative effects. We further examine the long-time behavior of the field propagator, characterizing its asymptotic structure and departures from flat-spacetime results. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for trans-Planckian physics, where the interplay between high-energy modes and cosmological expansion becomes particularly significant. Our results highlight the subtle role of background dynamics in shaping particle stability and propagation in the early universe.
